newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to reject French textiles state aid scheme.
newsitem.headline: EU to reject French textiles state aid scheme.

text.p: The European Commission is set to reject on Wednesday a French state aid scheme used to stem job losses in the textiles sector, a European Union source said on Tuesday.
"We will take the final negative decision," he told Reuters.

The Commission warned in March that it was set to veto the plan because it took a sectoral approach rather than applying general measures to preserve jobs. But it delayed the final decision twice to give France time to make changes.

French Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said on Tuesday that he planned to extend the scheme, which offers subsidies in the form of relief on payroll charges, and he hoped the Commission would at least offer a stay of execution on Wednesday.
But the EU source said the Commission was not entirely happy with what France had offered so far. "What they have presented us with to now is still not totally satisfactory," he said.
He said the Commission did not want to drag out the decision any longer, noting that it had received at least 15 complaints about the plan from EU governments and professional bodies.
The French plan was expected to save textile, clothing, shoe and leather companies 2.1 billion French francs ($365.2 million) in social security contributions over two years.
The Commission decision will affect about 1,700 companies out of 13,000 that are targeted for aid. The others are not affected because they are smaller companies receiving small amounts of aid.

The Commission has consistently opposed sectoral aid, arguing it distorts competition in the EU's border-free market. It cleared a Belgian scheme to cut social security charges on manual workers' wages in March after banning a previous scheme that gave tax breaks to export-led companies only.

Barrot told a news conference the French aid had so far preserved 35,000 jobs, or half those that would have been lost in an industry plunged into difficulty by cheaper imports from rivals in countries whose currencies had fallen against the franc.
He said it was too early to put a price on extension of the current scheme but said it would clearly be constrained by the need for a disciplined 1998 budget. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
